summary:
We developed Interesting Data Monitoring & Analysis, an interactive app that lets users explore Earth system temperature trends across three critical regions: the Amazon watersheds, the Arctic, and Antarctica. Each region is available as its own option, showing a graph of temperature anomalies over time along with an analysis of what the data reveals.

The app addresses the challenge by turning complex NASA Earth observation data into clear, visual insights. Instead of working with raw datasets, users can quickly see how temperatures deviate from long-term averages and identify warming trends, patterns, and unusual changes in each region.

This matters because the Amazon, Arctic, and Antarctica play a key role in regulating the global climate, and they are among the areas most sensitive to change. By making this data easy to explore and understand, our app helps students, researchers, and communities become “Earth system trend detectives” and take informed action on climate change.
details:
IDMA (Interesting Data Monitoring and Analysis) is a desktop application that turns NASA satellite and model data into a clear answer to one question: is this region really changing, and how confident are we? The user opens a world map and clicks a region: the Arctic, the Amazon river basin, Antarctica, or the Earth as a whole. The app then opens a time series of monthly surface air temperature anomaly from 1982 to 2026, together with an automatically generated plain-language interpretation of the trend. The user can zoom into any period by selecting an area of the chart with the mouse.

The time series come from NASA Giovanni (FLDAS Noah, monthly, 0.1°) and are area-averaged over each region. For every series the app estimates the rate of change and tests its significance with several independent methods: ordinary least squares with a t-test on the slope, the Mann-Kendall test, Sen’s slope, and confidence intervals for the rate of change (from regression, with an autocorrelation correction, and with a block bootstrap). Each test is run on both monthly and annual data. If all methods agree, the trend is reported as robust; if they disagree or the intervals include zero, the app says so. As a result, one planet produces very different regional signals. The Amazon and the Arctic show clear, statistically significant warming, with the Amazon peaking during the 2023–2024 drought, and the global land series shows persistent significant warming. Antarctica shows no statistically significant long-term trend: its slope is near zero, its sign depends on the method, and all confidence intervals span zero. Because the app reports “no trend” as readily as “trend”, it does not simply confirm what users expect.

The project lets students, educators and researchers check whether a trend is statistically real without writing code or digging through Giovanni. By showing the evidence and its limits, it teaches scientific thinking rather than just displaying a graph. Our next steps are a live connection to NASA Earthdata, user-drawn regions anywhere on Earth, additional variables such as ozone, sea ice and precipitation, and seasonal Mann-Kendall anomaly alerts. We built the project in Visual Studio using С#, NASA Giovanni data (FLDAS Noah, MERRA-2), and GitHub.

The project is creative in how it presents the analysis. The map is the interface: every label is a button, so exploring needs no menus or training, and next to each chart the app writes its own interpretation of the statistics in plain language. We included Antarctica on purpose, because a “no significant trend” result next to strong warming elsewhere is the clearest demonstration of why regional, localized testing matters. Along the way we considered several methodological factors: we used anomalies to remove seasonality, relied on Sen’s slope and nonparametric tests so that outliers do not drive the result, corrected for autocorrelation in the monthly data, and compared regions only through overlapping confidence intervals, without claiming differences the data cannot support.
